title: IELTS Academic – Đề tự soạn số 1
intro:
ĐỀ THI THỬ TỰ SOẠN – mô phỏng cấu trúc, dạng câu hỏi và độ khó của bài thi IELTS Academic. Đây KHÔNG phải đề thi thật; toàn bộ bài nghe, bài đọc, đề viết và câu hỏi nói đều do Trung tâm tự viết, không trích từ sách hay đề đã xuất bản.

CẤU TRÚC & THỜI GIAN (tổng khoảng 165 phút):
• Listening – khoảng 30 phút, 4 phần, 40 câu. Bài nghe chỉ phát MỘT lần như thi thật; đọc trước câu hỏi trước khi bấm nghe. (Thi giấy có thêm 10 phút chép đáp án, thi máy có 2 phút soát lại.)
• Reading – 60 phút, 3 bài đọc, 40 câu (13 + 13 + 14). Không có thêm giờ chép đáp án; nên dành khoảng 17–20 phút cho mỗi bài.
• Writing – 60 phút: Task 1 (mô tả biểu đồ, ít nhất 150 từ, nên dành 20 phút) và Task 2 (nghị luận, ít nhất 250 từ, nên dành 40 phút). Task 2 có trọng số gấp đôi Task 1.
• Speaking – 11–14 phút: Part 1 (4–5 phút, câu hỏi về bản thân), Part 2 (1 phút chuẩn bị + nói 1–2 phút theo thẻ đề), Part 3 (4–5 phút, thảo luận mở rộng).

QUY ĐỔI BAND (tham khảo, xấp xỉ – bảng thật xê dịch nhẹ tuỳ độ khó từng đề):
• Listening (số câu đúng/40): 39–40 → 9.0 · 37–38 → 8.5 · 35–36 → 8.0 · 32–34 → 7.5 · 30–31 → 7.0 · 26–29 → 6.5 · 23–25 → 6.0 · 18–22 → 5.5 · 16–17 → 5.0 · 13–15 → 4.5 · 10–12 → 4.0.
• Reading Academic (số câu đúng/40): 39–40 → 9.0 · 37–38 → 8.5 · 35–36 → 8.0 · 33–34 → 7.5 · 30–32 → 7.0 · 27–29 → 6.5 · 23–26 → 6.0 · 19–22 → 5.5 · 15–18 → 5.0 · 13–14 → 4.5 · 10–12 → 4.0.
• Writing: tự chấm mỗi task theo 4 tiêu chí (mỗi tiêu chí 0–9, lấy trung bình), rồi tính band Writing = (Task 1 + 2 × Task 2) ÷ 3.
• Speaking: tự chấm theo 4 tiêu chí (trôi chảy & mạch lạc, từ vựng, ngữ pháp, phát âm), lấy trung bình. Nên ghi âm và nghe lại để chấm khách quan hơn.
• Overall = trung bình cộng 4 kỹ năng, làm tròn đến 0.5 gần nhất: phần lẻ dưới .25 làm tròn xuống, .25 → .5, .75 → lên số nguyên. Ví dụ: (6.5 + 6.5 + 5.5 + 6.0) ÷ 4 = 6.125 → 6.0; (7.0 + 6.5 + 6.0 + 6.5) ÷ 4 = 6.5 → 6.5; (7.5 + 7.0 + 6.5 + 6.0) ÷ 4 = 6.75 → 7.0.

LƯU Ý KHI LÀM BÀI:
• Câu điền từ: viết sai chính tả hoặc vượt quá giới hạn số từ đều bị tính SAI. Đọc kỹ yêu cầu “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER”, “ONE WORD ONLY”…
• Người nói thường đổi ý hoặc nhắc tới nhiều thông tin gây nhiễu – đáp án là thông tin CUỐI CÙNG được xác nhận.
• TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN hỏi về THÔNG TIN trong bài; YES/NO/NOT GIVEN hỏi về QUAN ĐIỂM của tác giả.
• Mỗi câu tự chấm đều có giải thích tiếng Việt chỉ ra câu chứa đáp án – hãy xem lại kỹ các câu sai để rút kinh nghiệm.

sections.intro: Bạn sẽ nghe một cuộc điện thoại giữa một phụ nữ và nhân viên của thư viện cho mượn dụng cụ (tool library). Hoàn thành mẫu đơn bên dưới. Viết KHÔNG QUÁ HAI TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ cho mỗi chỗ trống (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER). Ví dụ đã cho sẵn: Membership type – household. Đọc kỹ câu 1–10 trước khi nghe; chú ý các chỗ người nói đổi ý.

dialog.note: Questions 1–10. Hillcrest Tool Library – New member form.

lines.t: Good morning, Hillcrest Tool Library. Adrian speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'd like to become a member, if that's possible. A friend of mine told me you lend out things like drills and garden equipment.
That's right. We've got over four hundred tools on our shelves now. I can take your details over the phone, and then you just pop in to collect your membership card. Is that all right?
Yes, that would be perfect.
Lovely. First of all, would you like an individual membership or a household one?
Household, please. To be honest, my partner will probably use it more than I will.
Household it is. Could I have your surname, please?
Yes, it's Whitcombe. That's W, H, I, T, C, O, M, B, E.
Thank you. And your first name?
Jenny.
And what's your address, Jenny?
It's fourteen Moorland Road. That's Moorland, all one word.
Fourteen Moorland Road. Is that the road just behind the swimming pool?
Yes, that's the one.
Great. And what's the best number to reach you on?
My mobile, I think. It's oh, seven, nine, two, three.
Yes.
Four, one, eight, double five, six.
So that's oh, seven, nine, two, three, four, one, eight, five, five, six.
That's right.
Now, we ask every member to choose a regular day for collecting and returning tools. It helps our volunteers plan. We're open on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.
Thursday would probably be easiest. Oh, hang on. I've just remembered that I'm working late on Thursdays from next month. Could you put me down for Saturday instead?
No problem at all. Saturday. And may I ask how you first heard about us? We like to know which kind of publicity works best.
Well, my friend recommended you, as I said. But actually, the first time I heard about the library was a few weeks before that. One of your volunteers was interviewed on the local radio.
Oh, that was me! I was terribly nervous. Right, now the fee. The standard annual fee is thirty-five pounds, but for people who live within the borough of Hillcrest, it's reduced to twenty-eight.
Moorland Road is definitely in the borough, so that's good news.

Then it's twenty-eight pounds, and you can pay when you collect your card. When you come in, please also bring something that proves your address. I'm afraid a driving licence isn't enough. We need to see a utility bill, and it should be less than three months old.
Fine. I'll find one.
Do you know what you'd like to borrow first?
We were going to ask for a ladder, because we're painting the hallway, but my brother has offered to lend us his. So I think it'll be the pressure washer. Our patio is completely green.

That's one of our most popular items. Normally, members can keep tools for seven days, but larger machines, like the pressure washer, can only be borrowed for four days, because there's usually a waiting list.
Four days will be plenty.
And one last thing. Before you take home any power tool, you'll need to watch a short safety video. It lasts about ten minutes, and you can watch it here at the library.
That sounds very sensible.
Great. We'll see you on Saturday, then.
Thanks very much. Bye.

items.q: Surname: ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: Jenny đánh vần: “It's Whitcombe. That's W, H, I, T, C, O, M, B, E.” Phải viết đúng từng chữ cái (hoa hay thường đều được). Bẫy chính tả: có chữ e câm ở cuối – viết “Whitcomb” là SAI.

items.q: Address: 14 ___ Road (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: “It's fourteen Moorland Road. That's Moorland, all one word.” → viết liền một từ. Chi tiết “just behind the swimming pool” chỉ là thông tin phụ, không cần ghi.

items.q: Mobile number: ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: “It's oh, seven, nine, two, three … Four, one, eight, double five, six.” Ghi nhớ: oh = số 0, double five = 55. Adrian đọc lại để xác nhận: 07923 418556.

items.q: Preferred day for collecting tools: ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: Bẫy ĐỔI Ý: Jenny nói “Thursday would probably be easiest” rồi sửa lại: “Could you put me down for Saturday instead?” → đáp án cuối cùng là Saturday, không phải Thursday.

items.q: First heard about the library on the local ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: Người bạn giới thiệu là chuyện SAU (bẫy). “the first time I heard about the library was a few weeks before that. One of your volunteers was interviewed on the local radio.” → radio.

items.q: Annual fee for borough residents: £___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: £35 là phí chuẩn (bẫy). “for people who live within the borough of Hillcrest, it's reduced to twenty-eight”, và Jenny ở trong borough → £28.

items.q: Proof of address: a ___ (less than three months old) (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: “I'm afraid a driving licence isn't enough. We need to see a utility bill, and it should be less than three months old.” Driving licence bị loại (bẫy). Utility bill = hoá đơn điện/nước/ga.

items.q: First item to borrow: a ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: Ban đầu định mượn ladder (thang) nhưng anh trai đã cho mượn: “So I think it'll be the pressure washer.” → máy rửa áp lực.

items.q: Maximum loan period for large machines: ___ days (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: “Normally, members can keep tools for seven days, but larger machines, like the pressure washer, can only be borrowed for four days” → 4. Bảy ngày là thời hạn cho dụng cụ thường (bẫy).

items.q: Before taking home a power tool: watch a short safety ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: “Before you take home any power tool, you'll need to watch a short safety video.” → video. Con số “about ten minutes” là thời lượng, không phải đáp án.

sections.intro: Bạn sẽ nghe điều phối viên tình nguyện của một khu bảo tồn đầm lầy ven biển hướng dẫn cho nhóm tình nguyện viên mới. Câu 11–15: chọn đáp án đúng A, B hoặc C. Câu 16–20: người nói nhận xét gì về mỗi khu vực? Chọn A–F (có 1 lựa chọn thừa).

dialog.note: Questions 11–20. Saltmarsh Point Nature Reserve – volunteer induction talk.

lines.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Saltmarsh Point Nature Reserve. My name's Megan, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. Thank you all for giving up your time. I'm going to tell you a little about the reserve and what you'll be doing, and then I'll describe the main areas you'll be working in.

Let me start with a bit of history. A lot of visitors assume that the reserve was bought by the government to protect wildlife, and some have heard that a wealthy local family donated the land. In fact, neither story is true. Until the late nineteen-eighties, this whole area was farmland. Then, during a severe winter storm, the old sea wall collapsed and seawater poured into the fields. The farmers decided that repairing the wall would cost too much, and within a few years the land had turned into the salt marsh you can see today. Only after that did the wildlife trust take over its management.

Now, your first day. I know many of you are keen to start counting birds, and you will, but bird surveys are only carried out by volunteers who've completed our identification course, which starts next month. So on your first day, you'll be working with our ranger, pulling out a shrub called sea buckthorn, which is spreading far too quickly and crowding out the native plants.

A quick word about clothing. Until last year, we kept a supply of rubber boots in the office for volunteers to borrow, but so many pairs went missing that we've had to stop. So please make sure you bring your own waterproof footwear. You'll each be given a green volunteer jacket, but you only need to wear it when you're leading a group of visitors.

Something else to bear in mind is the tide. Twice a day, the sea comes right up the creek, and the lower path, the one that leads out to the seal platform, disappears under water. People have been cut off before, so always check the tide timetable on the noticeboard before you set off.

As for benefits, everyone gets ten per cent off in the shop from their very first day. Once you've completed fifty hours of volunteering, we'll give you a free annual parking pass, which saves quite a lot of money. And if you ever need a reference letter for a job or a course, just ask. We're happy to write one, however many hours you've done.

Right, let me take you round the main areas. First, the Heron Hide, on the eastern bank. Visitors often tell us it's the best place to watch birds at sunrise, but in our experience the late afternoon is far better, because the sun is behind you. The hide was badly damaged in a storm two winters ago, and it was completely rebuilt last autumn, so it's in excellent condition now. Unfortunately, it's at the top of a steep slope, so it isn't suitable for wheelchairs.

If you have visitors with limited mobility, send them along the Boardwalk instead. It's completely flat, it's wide enough for two wheelchairs to pass each other, and it takes you right into the middle of the marsh.
The Reed Bed Trail is lovely, but please remember that it's closed from April to July while the birds are nesting, so don't direct visitors there in spring or early summer.

Then there's the Seal Platform, at the end of the lower path. There's only room for about twelve people at a time, so visitors have to reserve a place at the visitor centre before they walk out there.

And finally, the café beside the car park. Many people think it belongs to the reserve, but it's actually run by a local charity that trains young people for jobs in catering. So if anyone complains about the sandwiches, please send them to the charity, not to me! Right, does anyone have any questions so far?

items.q: According to Megan, how was the reserve created?
o: A. The government bought the land to protect wildlife.
B. Farmland flooded after the sea wall broke in a storm.
C. A local family gave the land to the wildlife trust.
items.e: Megan bác bỏ cả hai giả thuyết A và C: “In fact, neither story is true.” Sau đó: “during a severe winter storm, the old sea wall collapsed and seawater poured into the fields” → B (‘broke’ là cách nói khác của ‘collapsed’).

items.q: On their first day, the new volunteers will
o: A. count the birds on the marsh.
B. attend a bird identification course.
C. remove a plant that is spreading too fast.
items.e: “bird surveys are only carried out by volunteers who've completed our identification course, which starts next month. So on your first day, you'll be … pulling out a shrub called sea buckthorn, which is spreading far too quickly” → C. A và B là việc của tháng sau.

items.q: What does Megan say about clothing?
o: A. Volunteers need to bring their own waterproof footwear.
B. Rubber boots can be borrowed from the office.
C. The green jacket must be worn at all times.
items.e: Trước đây có cho mượn ủng nhưng đã ngừng (bẫy B): “so many pairs went missing that we've had to stop. So please make sure you bring your own waterproof footwear.” → A. Áo khoác xanh chỉ mặc khi dẫn đoàn (“only … when you're leading a group”) → C sai.

items.q: Why must volunteers check the tide timetable?
o: A. Part of a path can be covered by the sea.
B. The seals can only be seen at high tide.
C. The visitor centre closes at high tide.
items.e: “the lower path, the one that leads out to the seal platform, disappears under water. People have been cut off before, so always check the tide timetable” → A.

items.q: What will volunteers receive after completing fifty hours?
o: A. a discount in the shop
items.e: Giảm giá 10% có ngay “from their very first day” (A sai); thư giới thiệu viết “however many hours you've done” (B sai). “Once you've completed fifty hours … we'll give you a free annual parking pass” → C.

items.q: What does Megan say about the Heron Hide?
o: A. closed for part of the year
D. must be booked in advance
E. best visited early in the morning
F. run by a different organisation
items.e: “it was completely rebuilt last autumn” → C. Bẫy E: khách hay nói xem lúc bình minh là tốt nhất, nhưng Megan khẳng định “the late afternoon is far better”. Bẫy B: “it isn't suitable for wheelchairs”.

items.q: What does Megan say about the Boardwalk?
o: A. closed for part of the year
D. must be booked in advance
E. best visited early in the morning
F. run by a different organisation
items.e: “If you have visitors with limited mobility, send them along the Boardwalk instead. It's completely flat, it's wide enough for two wheelchairs…” → B.

items.q: What does Megan say about the Reed Bed Trail?
o: A. closed for part of the year
D. must be booked in advance
E. best visited early in the morning
F. run by a different organisation
items.e: “it's closed from April to July while the birds are nesting” → đóng cửa một phần trong năm → A.

items.q: What does Megan say about the Seal Platform?
o: A. closed for part of the year
D. must be booked in advance
E. best visited early in the morning
F. run by a different organisation
items.e: “There's only room for about twelve people at a time, so visitors have to reserve a place at the visitor centre before they walk out there.” ‘reserve a place’ = ‘book in advance’ → D.

items.q: What does Megan say about the café?
o: A. closed for part of the year
D. must be booked in advance
E. best visited early in the morning
F. run by a different organisation
items.e: “Many people think it belongs to the reserve, but it's actually run by a local charity” → do một tổ chức khác điều hành → F. (Lựa chọn E không dùng cho khu nào.)

sections.intro: Bạn sẽ nghe hai sinh viên ngành môi trường, Hannah và Oscar, bàn về bài thuyết trình về mái nhà xanh (green roofs). Câu 21–25: chọn A, B hoặc C. Câu 26–30: hai bạn nhận xét gì về từng nguồn tài liệu? Chọn A–F (có 1 lựa chọn thừa).

dialog.note: Questions 21–30. Two students discuss their seminar presentation on green roofs.

lines.t: Hi, Hannah. Have you got a few minutes to go through our presentation on green roofs? It's only two weeks away now.
Sure. I was going to suggest the same thing. Shall we start with why we chose the topic? Doctor Barnes wants us to explain that in the introduction.
Well, I always assumed it was on the list of topics he gave us.

No, it wasn't, actually. His list had things like flood barriers and solar farms. I suggested green roofs because I'd spent most of the spring watching the builders put one on top of the new sports hall, right opposite my window. I got quite fascinated by it.
Oh, of course, I'd forgotten that. I'd hoped my summer job at the recycling centre might be relevant too, but it really isn't.
OK, so then the survey. We asked sixty residents in the Eastfield area what they thought about having green roofs on their buildings.
To be honest, I wasn't surprised that hardly anyone had heard of the term green roof.

Me neither. But what I really didn't expect was the age difference. I'd assumed younger people would be the keenest, but it was the over-sixties who were the most enthusiastic. Lots of them talked about wanting more green space and somewhere to sit outside.
Yes, that was interesting. Now, the temperature data. That's the part I'm worried about.
Because two of the sensors stopped working?

No, we replaced those quickly, so we didn't lose much. The real issue is that we measured the green roof at midday, but the readings from the ordinary roof next door were taken in the evening, after the caretaker had unlocked the stairs. So the two sets of figures can't really be compared directly.
Hmm. I suppose we'll just have to be honest about that and present it as a limitation.
Agreed. Now, how are we going to begin? I thought we could put up that photo of the sports hall roof covered in wildflowers.
It's a lovely picture, but everybody starts with a photo. What about a striking statistic, like how much hotter city centres are than the countryside?
We've got lots of numbers later on, though. What if we open by asking the audience how many of them have ever actually stood on a green roof? Then we show the photo straight after.
Yes, that's much more engaging. Let's do that.
And then there's the section on costs. At the moment it's five slides long.
That's far too much. I don't think we need to ask Doctor Barnes about it. Let's just cut it down to one slide with the key figures.
Fine. Then we need to say what we thought of each of our sources.
Right. The city council report first.
I found it really dull to read.
Maybe, but it has the most reliable local data. I think almost everything we say should be based on it.
Fair enough. That's our main source, then. What about the television documentary?

It was beautifully filmed, but I checked some of the numbers. It says forty per cent of the city's roofs are green, when the real figure is four per cent. There are mistakes like that all the way through.
Not one to rely on, then. And the chapter from the textbook?
The library copy was easy enough to get hold of, but it was written over fifteen years ago, before most of the new materials existed. So a lot of it no longer applies.
Then there's the interview with the building manager at the sports hall.
I liked him, but he was quite negative. He kept talking about leaks and maintenance costs.
But that's useful, isn't it? Everything else we've read is so positive. His view gives the presentation some balance.
True. And finally, that online gardening forum.
Lots of people chatting about roof gardens in general, but nothing specific about cities or temperature. I don't think it adds much.
No, it's far too broad for what we need. Let's just list it as background reading.

items.q: Why did the students choose green roofs as their topic?
o: A. Hannah had watched one being built.
B. It was on a list of topics from their tutor.
C. It was connected with Oscar's summer job.
items.e: Hannah phủ nhận B: “No, it wasn't, actually.” Lý do thật: “I'd spent most of the spring watching the builders put one on top of the new sports hall” → A. Oscar tự nói việc làm hè “really isn't” liên quan → C sai.

items.q: What surprised Hannah about the survey results?
o: A. Very few residents knew the term ‘green roof’.
B. Most residents were worried about the cost.
C. Older residents were the most enthusiastic.
items.e: Về A cả hai nói “I wasn't surprised” – “Me neither” (không bất ngờ). B không được nhắc tới. Điều bất ngờ: “what I really didn't expect was the age difference … it was the over-sixties who were the most enthusiastic” → C.

items.q: What is the main problem with the temperature data?
o: A. Some of the sensors broke down.
B. The two roofs were measured at different times of day.
C. Too few measurements were taken.
items.e: Cảm biến hỏng đã được thay ngay (“we replaced those quickly”) → A không phải vấn đề chính. “The real issue is that we measured the green roof at midday, but the readings from the ordinary roof … were taken in the evening” → B.

items.q: How will the students begin their presentation?
o: C. with a question for the audience
items.e: Oscar đề xuất ảnh, Hannah đề xuất số liệu, cuối cùng chốt: “What if we open by asking the audience how many of them have ever actually stood on a green roof? Then we show the photo straight after.” – “Yes … Let's do that.” → mở đầu bằng câu hỏi (C); ảnh chiếu SAU.

items.q: What do the students decide to do about the section on costs?
o: A. reduce it to a single slide
B. ask their tutor for advice
C. move it to the end of the talk
items.e: “I don't think we need to ask Doctor Barnes about it” → B sai. “Let's just cut it down to one slide with the key figures.” → A.

items.q: What do the students say about the city council report?
o: C. offers an opposing point of view
D. too general to be useful
E. will be their main source
items.e: Oscar thấy chán (dull) nhưng Hannah: “it has the most reliable local data … almost everything we say should be based on it” và Oscar chốt: “That's our main source, then.” → E.

items.q: What do the students say about the television documentary?
o: C. offers an opposing point of view
D. too general to be useful
E. will be their main source
items.e: “It says forty per cent of the city's roofs are green, when the real figure is four per cent. There are mistakes like that all the way through.” → B.

items.q: What do the students say about the textbook chapter?
o: C. offers an opposing point of view
D. too general to be useful
E. will be their main source
items.e: Bẫy F: sách “easy enough to get hold of” (dễ kiếm). Vấn đề là “it was written over fifteen years ago … a lot of it no longer applies” → lỗi thời → A.

items.q: What do the students say about the interview with the building manager?
o: C. offers an opposing point of view
D. too general to be useful
E. will be their main source
items.e: Ông ấy nói nhiều mặt tiêu cực (rò rỉ, chi phí bảo trì); Oscar: “Everything else we've read is so positive. His view gives the presentation some balance.” → quan điểm trái chiều → C.

items.q: What do the students say about the online gardening forum?
o: C. offers an opposing point of view
D. too general to be useful
E. will be their main source
items.e: “roof gardens in general, but nothing specific about cities or temperature” – “it's far too broad for what we need” → quá chung chung → D. (Lựa chọn F không dùng.)

lines.t: Today I will describe the making of a small lighting display for the fictional Orelan Sound classroom exhibition. This is a design exercise, not the history of a real invention. Our group wanted visitors to notice the changing outlines on a wall without having to touch the display. We began by drawing a map of the room. The map showed the entrance, the viewing point and the route back out, so the display could be considered in relation to the people using the space.
lines.vi: Hôm nay nói thiết kế đèn cho trưng bày Orelan Sound hư cấu, không lịch sử phát minh. Nhóm muốn khách nhìn hình viền đổi trên tường mà không chạm. Sơ đồ đầu ghi cửa, điểm xem và lối ra để xét vật theo người dùng.

lines.t: Our first visual effect was a moving shadow. We used that word carefully: the dark shape on the wall was not a picture printed on the wall itself. It appeared when a screen changed the path of the light in our classroom model. At first, several visitors looked at the screen rather than the wall, so the guide added a short introduction explaining where to look. We did not treat that instruction as evidence that the display was already clear to everyone.
lines.vi: Hiệu ứng đầu là bóng chuyển, không ảnh in tường. Trong mô hình lớp, màn đổi đường sáng tạo hình tối. Vài khách nhìn màn thay tường nên người dẫn thêm câu chỉ chỗ nhìn; câu chỉ dẫn chưa chứng mọi người đều hiểu.

lines.t: For the screen, the team chose paper rather than cloth. The choice belonged to this model and the materials we had available; we were not recommending paper for every lighting project. Each sheet carried a small identification mark. If two trial versions looked similar, the mark helped us connect the visitor’s comment to the correct version. Without that link, a detailed opinion could be recorded against the wrong object, making the later comparison less useful.
lines.vi: Màn dùng giấy thay vải theo vật liệu của mô hình, không khuyên mọi dự án đèn. Mỗi tờ có dấu nhận diện để nối ý khách với đúng phiên bản, tránh ghi nhận xét chi tiết vào nhầm vật.

lines.t: Next, we compared the folds in the paper. One arrangement was easy to assemble but difficult to reset after a demonstration. Another required more preparation but could be returned to its starting position consistently. The group kept notes on both, rather than calling the quickest assembly the best design. We also recorded who performed the task. A version that seemed simple to its maker might still need explanation when another student tried it for the first time.
lines.vi: Nhóm so nếp gấp: loại lắp dễ nhưng đặt lại khó, loại chuẩn bị lâu hơn mà trở về vị trí đầu đều hơn. Ghi cả hai và ai làm, không gọi lắp nhanh nhất là tốt nhất; người làm quen có thể thấy dễ hơn người mới.

lines.t: The viewing angle was another concern. From the position nearest the door, the changing shape was partly hidden by a partition. Moving the entire display would have used space needed for the return route. We therefore tried a different viewing point first. This was a limited adjustment with a clear reason, not a complete redesign. The report named the angle as the issue being tested, so readers would not mistake a change in position for a change in the screen itself.
lines.vi: Góc nhìn gần cửa bị vách che một phần. Dời cả trưng bày chiếm lối ra nên thử điểm nhìn khác trước. Báo cáo nêu góc là vấn đề kiểm để không tưởng nhóm đổi màn.

lines.t: We then wrote labels for the objects and the sequence. The first label was long, yet it did not say which action belonged to the guide and which belonged to the visitor. A shorter version named the actor at each step. We kept the discarded label in our teaching folder because it showed the problem we had found. Preserving it did not mean that it remained an approved instruction for the next demonstration.
lines.vi: Nhãn đầu dài nhưng chưa rõ việc người dẫn và khách. Bản ngắn gọi đúng người từng bước. Giữ nhãn bỏ trong hồ sơ học để thấy vấn đề, không coi nó còn được duyệt dùng.

lines.t: Before opening the room, the group ran a trial with a few classmates. We asked them where they looked first, what they expected to happen and which part of the explanation they wanted repeated. We did not ask whether they liked the exhibition and use that one answer to infer everything else. A favourable opinion could coexist with a misunderstanding of the sequence. Recording different questions separately made the remaining work easier to identify.
lines.vi: Trước mở nhóm thử với vài bạn, hỏi chỗ nhìn đầu, kỳ vọng và phần muốn nhắc lại. Không lấy một lời thích để suy mọi điều khác; thích vẫn có thể hiểu nhầm trình tự. Ghi riêng để thấy việc còn lại.

lines.t: Finally, the display needed a member of staff during the activity. Our notes called this person the duty guide. The role included welcoming the group, describing the sequence and recording questions that could not yet be answered. We ended by fixing a review date rather than declaring the design finished forever. The review would include another guide, so that the original maker would not be the only person deciding whether the explanation was clear. On that date, we would compare the comments with the version marks and decide which change to retain. The exhibition was ready for a limited classroom use, with its support arrangements stated alongside it.

read.title: From Three Recipe Cards to a Traceable Edition – original case
read.text:
[A] The fictional Ruvan Table project began when Nera brought three handwritten recipe cards to a family recording activity. She wanted to create a booklet that younger relatives could use without asking someone to explain every line. The cards looked familiar, but they did not contain one stable set of instructions. An ingredient appeared in a margin on one copy, a quantity had been crossed out on another, and the third ended before the final stage. The group soon found that recording a recipe meant more than typing the most readable page.

[B] Their first decision concerned the word original. The oldest surviving card was not necessarily the first version ever used, and nobody could identify a single person who had invented the dish. Some relatives remembered preparing it differently from what the card described. Nera therefore used earliest surviving copy rather than original recipe in the draft. That distinction did not make the old card unimportant. It prevented the booklet from presenting one surviving object as a complete history that the group had not actually established.

[C] The team then asked two relatives to explain the same stage separately. One measured a small amount with a spoon; the other judged it from the texture of the mixture. Their accounts were not immediately compatible, but the group did not average the two and pretend it had obtained a third inherited method. Instead, the booklet would identify the person associated with each version. A reader could then see which instruction came from which account and ask a more specific question if the result was unclear.

[D] A trial exposed another problem. Tavin, who had not watched the earlier conversations, followed the typed draft and stopped at an instruction to add the remaining liquid. The draft had not said how much liquid should have been kept back, so remaining depended on knowledge he did not have. The team could not solve this by making the wording more formal. They had to restore a missing relation between stages. The revised account stated when a portion was set aside and named the later action in which it would be used.

[E] Illustrations helped with one task but created a different risk. A drawing showed how the mixture looked at a particular stage, allowing a novice to compare it with the bowl in front of them. Yet a reader might assume that the pictured colour was the only acceptable one. The group added a caption explaining what the picture was intended to demonstrate and which features were not being used as a test. The drawing remained useful because its purpose became narrower, rather than because the team claimed that a picture could replace every explanation.

[F] The booklet also had to distinguish a family account from practical food-safety advice. A remembered habit was not presented as proof that a method was safe, and the project did not invent storage limits or cooking temperatures. Questions requiring such guidance were marked for appropriate checking outside this language exercise. Within the booklet, the team concentrated on attribution, sequence and the meaning of quantities. This boundary allowed the class to discuss inherited knowledge without turning every memory into an instruction that readers were expected to apply without further thought.

[G] At the final review, the group kept the three card images beside the edited versions. They recorded where a sentence had been clarified and where disagreement remained. The booklet could now help a new reader follow an account, but it did not claim to preserve every family practice or settle the ownership of a dish. Nera described the result as a traceable edition: readers could move from a clear instruction back to the particular card, explanation or editorial decision supporting it. A short index connected each edited page to the card or conversation from which its details came. The project’s success lay in making that route visible, not in removing all variation from the food or all uncertainty from its story.
read.vi: Dự án gia đình Ruvan Table hư cấu có ba thẻ công thức khác và thiếu bước. Tavin chưa nghe trao đổi nên vướng cụm phần chất lỏng còn lại: phải bổ bước giữ riêng trước đó. Ảnh có chú thích để không suy màu duy nhất đúng. Nhóm không biến ký ức thành hướng dẫn an toàn hay bịa giới hạn bảo quản/nhiệt độ. Bản cuối giữ ảnh thẻ và lý do sửa, gọi là ấn bản có thể lần căn cứ, không bảo xóa hết biến thể hoặc giải quyền sở hữu món.

read.title: Two Records for One Rehearsal Room – original classroom case
read.text:
[A] At the fictional Varel Nook rehearsal centre, a calendar once seemed sufficient for every kind of booking. Groups wrote their names beside a room and a time, and the caretaker copied the page before locking the office. This arrangement worked while a few familiar members made occasional requests. The difficulty emerged when more people began using the centre, some arriving through a written application and others speaking directly to a member who happened to be there. A mark on the calendar could mean several different things, although nobody had written those meanings down.

[B] The first serious confusion arose during a classroom production. One group had asked whether a room might be available, while another had already received confirmation for the same period. Both appeared on the calendar. The caretaker could not tell which entry represented a question and which represented an agreed commitment. Cancelling the larger group would not solve the underlying problem, because size had never been the rule for confirmation. The centre needed to identify the status of an entry before deciding what action should follow from it.

[C] Nera, the coordinator in this invented case, proposed two records. A request list would contain enquiries, missing details and the person expected to respond. A separate calendar would contain confirmed use. This was not simply a decision to create more paperwork. It made a transition visible: someone had to review a request and communicate a decision before transferring it. Nera added a daily checking period so that requests did not remain unanswered merely because the main calendar looked tidy. Each record would have a different purpose, and the relationship between them had to be explained.

[D] Members did not welcome every part of the change. Some worried that an informal conversation would no longer count, especially for people who found the written form difficult. Others disliked being asked for details that a familiar caretaker already knew. The proposal was revised to retain a spoken route. A named member could record a request on someone’s behalf, but that help would not itself confirm the booking. The change therefore kept a form of personal assistance while making its limits explicit. Familiarity could support communication without becoming an invisible alternative approval system.

[E] A small trial then compared completed requests, unanswered questions and errors in the confirmed calendar. The team found fewer duplicated entries, but it also noticed a longer wait before some decisions. The result presented a trade-off rather than a simple success story. One member suggested reporting only the duplication count because it looked encouraging. Nera kept the waiting record beside it. A system that prevents one error may still create another difficulty, and readers cannot judge the arrangement if a less favourable measure has quietly disappeared from the report.

[F] The next revision addressed responsibility rather than the number of records. Previously, several members assumed that another person would reply. The team appointed a duty reviewer and recorded when an unanswered request should be passed on. It also gave applicants a reference code that could be quoted when asking about progress. The code identified the request; it did not prove that the room had been granted. This distinction mattered because a helpful new device could otherwise repeat the original problem, allowing one visible mark to carry more authority than it actually had.

[G] At the end of the exercise, the centre retained both records with a date for review. It did not claim that every community group needed the same arrangement. A smaller group might work well with one record, provided the status and responsibilities remained clear. The lesson was not that additional forms automatically produce fairness or efficiency. It was that records need a stated purpose, transitions need an accountable actor and improvements need to be assessed against more than the measure that makes them look best. The class was asked to judge the proposal by these conditions, not by the neatness of the new calendar.

read.title: A Progress Board Is Also a Promise – original viewpoint
read.text:
The fictional Mela Thread repair room wants to publish a simple board showing the progress of customers’ items. Its members hope that visible stages will reduce repeated questions and make delays easier to discuss. I support that aim, but I doubt the claim that a public board automatically produces a trustworthy service. A record becomes useful when the meaning of each stage is shared. Without that work, greater visibility may simply spread an inaccurate promise to more people.

Consider the first label, received. To the member at the desk, it means that an item has entered the room and been given an identification card. To a customer, it may imply that someone has inspected it and accepted the repair. These are different events. The board should therefore separate receipt, assessment and agreement. This may make the route look less impressively short, but it allows people to see where a decision is still required. Hiding a stage does not remove the time or judgement needed to complete it.

The same problem appears with dates. A target date can help a customer plan, yet it should not be presented as a confirmed return date when assessment is incomplete. Merely adding the word provisional in small print is an inadequate response if the main display still looks definite. The meaning needs to appear where the customer makes the decision. That might require a short spoken explanation as well as a label. I would rather publish a qualified date that people understand than an apparently precise date whose status remains unclear.

There is a reasonable objection: too much qualification can make a board difficult to read. A page full of conditions may leave a customer less informed than a short conversation. However, this is not an argument for suppressing every condition. It is an argument for organising information in layers. The main board can show the current stage and whether the next date is a target or a commitment. A separate note can explain exceptions, while a named member remains available for questions that the display cannot answer.

Privacy creates another trade-off. Customers may want to find their items quickly, but they do not necessarily want their names or the details of a personal object displayed to everyone in the room. In this invented case, the team chooses reference numbers for the public board and keeps identifying details in a separate record. The number is a way to locate progress, not a judgement about a customer’s importance. This arrangement still requires care in conversation: reading out private details beside the board would undermine the separation the design was intended to create.

The team’s first trial finds fewer repeated enquiries, and one member proposes declaring the board a success. I would report the reduction while asking what it means. Perhaps customers understand the stages better; perhaps some have stopped asking because the board appears final. The count alone cannot decide between those explanations. A brief check of what customers expect to happen next would provide a different kind of evidence. A person who waits quietly may still misunderstand the next step, while a person who asks twice may have noticed a genuine ambiguity. These cases deserve separate attention rather than being treated simply as better or worse enquiry counts. The trial should also retain complaints and unresolved questions instead of counting only the interactions that make the new arrangement look convenient.

My conclusion is conditional rather than hostile. A public board may be a useful part of a repair service, provided it identifies stages honestly, protects personal details and leaves a visible route for clarification. It should support the work of responsible members rather than act as an excuse for saying that the answer is already on the wall. Trust is not created by displaying every detail or by making every statement certain. It grows when people can understand a promise, locate the person responsible for it and discover when the information needs to change.
read.vi: Tác giả ủng hộ bảng tiến độ tại phòng sửa Mela Thread hư cấu nhưng không coi nhìn thấy là tự tạo tin cậy. Phải tách nhận đồ, đánh giá, đồng ý; ngày mục tiêu khác cam kết và điều kiện phải ngay chỗ khách quyết. Phân tầng thông tin thay giấu mọi điều kiện. Dùng mã công khai, giữ chi tiết riêng ở hồ sơ khác và không đọc to làm mất tách biệt. Ít câu hỏi có thể do hiểu hơn hoặc ngại hỏi, cần kiểm kỳ vọng và giữ khiếu nại/câu chưa đáp. Bảng hữu ích khi trạng thái, lời hứa, người chịu trách nhiệm và đường hỏi rõ; nó hỗ trợ người làm chứ không thay trách nhiệm.

items.q: What is the writer’s view of the board’s general aim?
o: Certain that visibility alone guarantees trust.
Favourable only if questions are forbidden.
items.e: Đoạn đầu I support that aim nhưng nghi automatically trustworthy, nên hỗ trợ có điều kiện.

items.q: Why separate receipt, assessment and agreement?
o: The room has no identification cards.
Customers must never see a date.

o: It eliminates every need for assessment.
The main display may still imply certainty.
It always has no grammatical meaning.

sections.intro: Nên dành khoảng 20 phút. Viết ít nhất 150 từ. Viết xong, đếm số từ, tự chấm theo 4 tiêu chí bên dưới rồi so sánh với bài mẫu.

write.task:
The line graph below shows the proportion of households in Country X that used five different main heating systems between 1980 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Main heating system used by households in Country X, 1980–2020

write.model:
The line graph illustrates how the main type of heating used by households in Country X changed over the forty years between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, mains gas was by far the most widespread system throughout the period, while oil and solid fuel declined steadily. The most striking development, however, was the rapid take-up of heat pumps in the final decade.

In 1980, mains gas was already the leading system, heating 38% of homes, followed by oil (30%) and solid fuel (25%). Over the next three decades, the share of gas rose by more than 30 percentage points to a peak of 70% in 2010, before slipping back slightly to 66% in 2020. Oil and solid fuel moved in the opposite direction: the proportion of homes relying on oil fell continuously to just 8%, while solid fuel, used by a quarter of households at the start of the period, accounted for a mere 5% by the end.

Heat pumps were virtually non-existent in 1980 and remained marginal for the next thirty years, reaching only 5% by 2010. Over the following decade, however, this figure almost tripled to 14%, making heat pumps the second most common system in 2020. Electric storage heaters, by contrast, showed remarkable stability, fluctuating between 7% and 8% throughout.
tips: Bố cục 4 đoạn: (1) mở bài – diễn đạt lại đề, (2) overview – 2–3 xu hướng lớn nhất, KHÔNG có số liệu chi tiết, (3)–(4) thân bài – nhóm các đường có xu hướng giống nhau (tăng / giảm / ổn định).
Chọn lọc số liệu: điểm đầu, điểm cuối, đỉnh, đáy, các điểm giao nhau – không liệt kê lần lượt cả 25 con số.
Khi so sánh hai tỷ lệ phần trăm, dùng ‘percentage points’ (38% → 70% là tăng 32 percentage points, không phải 32%).
Không đưa ý kiến cá nhân hay giải thích nguyên nhân (ví dụ: vì sao heat pumps tăng) – Task 1 chỉ mô tả và so sánh.
rubric: Hoàn thành yêu cầu đề (Task Achievement): có đoạn tổng quan nêu đúng các xu hướng chính (gas dẫn đầu suốt giai đoạn; dầu và nhiên liệu rắn giảm đều; heat pumps tăng vọt thập kỷ cuối); số liệu chọn lọc, chính xác, có so sánh; không bịa thêm thông tin; đủ 150 từ.

Mạch lạc & liên kết (Coherence and Cohesion): chia đoạn theo nhóm xu hướng hợp lý; người đọc theo dõi dễ dàng; từ nối đa dạng nhưng tự nhiên (however, by contrast, meanwhile, over the following decade), dùng từ thay thế (this figure, the share of gas) để tránh lặp.

Vốn từ (Lexical Resource): diễn đạt xu hướng phong phú và chính xác (rise, slip back, fall continuously, peak at, remain marginal, fluctuate), dùng đúng proportion / share / percentage points; chính tả đúng.

Ngữ pháp (Grammatical Range and Accuracy): thì quá khứ cho số liệu đã qua; kết hợp câu đơn và câu phức (mệnh đề quan hệ, cụm phân từ ‘making heat pumps…’, ‘used by a quarter of households…’); so sánh hơn/nhất đúng; phần lớn câu không có lỗi.

Tự chấm nhanh: thiếu overview hoặc mô tả sai xu hướng → khó vượt band 5; có overview rõ, số liệu chọn lọc, còn vài lỗi nhỏ → khoảng band 7; mọi đặc điểm chính được nêu sắc nét, từ vựng linh hoạt, lỗi rất hiếm → band 8 trở lên.

write.task:
Some people believe that private cars should be banned from city centres, while others argue that such a ban would cause more problems than it solves.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
write.model:
In many cities, the central streets are congested for much of the day, and proposals to exclude private vehicles from them altogether have become increasingly common. While I accept that an outright ban could create genuine difficulties, I believe that, if it is introduced gradually and supported by good public transport, its benefits would far outweigh its costs.

Opponents of such a ban raise several legitimate concerns. The most obvious is accessibility: elderly people, those with disabilities and parents with young children may find it much harder to reach shops, clinics or workplaces without a car. Business owners, too, often fear that customers will simply drive to out-of-town shopping centres instead, leaving city-centre shops struggling to survive. There is also a risk that the traffic will not disappear but merely shift to the surrounding residential streets, making life worse for the people who live there.

Supporters, on the other hand, point to the considerable advantages of car-free centres. Removing private vehicles sharply reduces air pollution and noise, both of which are linked to respiratory illness and stress. It also frees up a remarkable amount of space: roads and car parks can be turned into pedestrian squares, cycle lanes and green areas, making the centre a more pleasant place to spend time. Contrary to shopkeepers' fears, a number of European cities that have pedestrianised their historic cores report that footfall, and with it trade, has actually increased.

In my view, the arguments in favour are more persuasive, but the objections should shape how a ban is implemented rather than whether it happens at all. Exemptions for disabled drivers, emergency services and deliveries at set times are essential, and any restriction must be preceded by investment in frequent, affordable buses or trams, as well as park-and-ride facilities on the edge of the city.

In conclusion, although banning private cars from city centres is not without its problems, a carefully planned ban would make cities cleaner, safer and more liveable, and it is therefore a change worth making.
tips: Dạng ‘Discuss both views and give your own opinion’: phải bàn CẢ HAI phía và nêu ý kiến riêng rõ ràng – tốt nhất ngay ở mở bài, nhắc lại ở kết bài.
Bố cục gợi ý: mở bài (bối cảnh + ý kiến) – thân bài 1 (quan điểm phản đối) – thân bài 2 (quan điểm ủng hộ) – thân bài 3 (ý kiến của bạn + điều kiện/giải pháp) – kết bài.
Mỗi luận điểm cần: câu chủ đề → giải thích vì sao → ví dụ hoặc hệ quả cụ thể. Một ý được phát triển kỹ tốt hơn ba ý liệt kê.
Tránh học thuộc câu mẫu sáo rỗng (‘In this day and age…’, ‘Every coin has two sides’) – giám khảo đánh giá thấp.
rubric: Trả lời đúng & đủ đề (Task Response): bàn cả hai quan điểm với mức độ phát triển tương xứng; ý kiến cá nhân rõ ràng, nhất quán từ mở bài đến kết bài; luận điểm có lý do và ví dụ cụ thể, không lạc đề; ít nhất 250 từ.

Mạch lạc & liên kết (Coherence and Cohesion): mỗi đoạn thân bài có một ý trung tâm và câu chủ đề rõ; ý sau nối ý trước một cách logic; liên kết bằng nội dung (such a ban, these concerns, this) thay vì chỉ dùng từ nối máy móc (Firstly, Moreover, Furthermore…).

Vốn từ (Lexical Resource): dùng collocation tự nhiên và chính xác (legitimate concerns, far outweigh, footfall, park-and-ride, not without its problems); diễn đạt lại ý của đề thay vì chép nguyên; không dùng từ ‘đao to búa lớn’ sai ngữ cảnh; chính tả đúng.
Ngữ pháp (Grammatical Range and Accuracy): đa dạng cấu trúc (câu điều kiện, mệnh đề quan hệ, bị động, nhượng bộ while/although, cụm phân từ) và dùng chính xác; dấu câu chuẩn; đa số câu không lỗi.

Tự chấm nhanh: chỉ bàn một phía hoặc không nêu ý kiến → Task Response khó vượt band 5; có ý kiến nhưng luận điểm chung chung, thiếu giải thích → khoảng band 6; luận điểm phát triển tốt, ý kiến nhất quán, lỗi ít → band 7; lập luận sắc, từ vựng tự nhiên, lỗi hiếm → band 8 trở lên.

sections.intro: Giám khảo hỏi các câu ngắn về bản thân theo 2 chủ đề quen thuộc. Trả lời tự nhiên trong khoảng 2–4 câu: trả lời thẳng → giải thích lý do → thêm ví dụ hoặc chi tiết. Ghi âm câu trả lời của bạn, nghe lại rồi so với câu mẫu (band 8).

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Mornings: Are you a morning person?
tasks.model: Honestly, I'd say I've gradually become one. When I was at university, I was a real night owl and could barely function before ten, but since I started working, I've found that the first couple of hours of the day are when my head is clearest, so I've learned to make the most of them.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Mornings: What do you usually do in the first hour after you wake up?
tasks.model: It's fairly predictable, really. I drink a big glass of water, make myself a strong coffee, and then I try to resist checking my phone for at least twenty minutes, which, to be fair, I don't always manage. If I have time, I'll go for a short walk around the lake near my flat before getting ready for work.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Mornings: Has your morning routine changed since you were a child?
tasks.model: Quite dramatically. As a kid, my mornings were completely organised by my mum: she'd wake me up, put breakfast in front of me and practically push me out of the door. These days I'm the one in charge, which means things are a bit more relaxed, but also, admittedly, a lot less reliable.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Mornings: Do you think it's important to eat breakfast?
tasks.model: I think it depends on the person. For me, skipping breakfast is a recipe for disaster, because by mid-morning I'm grumpy and can't concentrate. But I know plenty of people who feel perfectly fine until lunch, so I wouldn't say there's one rule that suits everybody.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Handwriting: Do you write by hand much these days?
tasks.model: Not nearly as much as I used to. Almost everything I write for work is typed, so my handwriting is mostly limited to shopping lists and the odd sticky note. The one exception is when I'm studying, because I still find that writing notes by hand helps things stick in my memory.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Handwriting: Is your handwriting easy to read?
tasks.model: That depends on how much of a hurry I'm in! When I take my time, it's reasonably neat, but when I'm scribbling notes in a meeting, it turns into something that even I struggle to decipher afterwards.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Handwriting: Should children still learn to write by hand at school?
tasks.model: Definitely. Even if they end up typing most things as adults, learning to form letters by hand helps develop fine motor skills, and many teachers believe it supports reading and memory as well. Besides, there will always be situations, like exams or filling in forms, where a keyboard simply isn't available.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Handwriting: Do you prefer receiving handwritten cards or digital messages?
tasks.model: Handwritten cards, without a doubt. A message on my phone is convenient, but it's forgotten in a second, whereas a card shows that someone has actually sat down and made an effort. I've kept a whole box of birthday cards from my grandparents, and I'd never dream of throwing them away.

rubric: Trôi chảy & mạch lạc (Fluency and Coherence): nói liền mạch, ít ngập ngừng vì tìm từ; câu trả lời có phát triển (trả lời → lý do → ví dụ) chứ không chỉ một câu cụt; dùng từ đệm và từ nối tự nhiên (honestly, to be fair, that said, besides).
Vốn từ (Lexical Resource): có cụm từ và thành ngữ tự nhiên, dùng đúng ngữ cảnh (a night owl, a recipe for disaster, make the most of, the odd sticky note); biết diễn đạt lại khi quên từ.
Ngữ pháp (Grammatical Range and Accuracy): kết hợp linh hoạt các thì (hiện tại hoàn thành để nói về thay đổi, would/used to cho thói quen trong quá khứ), câu phức, câu điều kiện; đa số câu không lỗi.
Phát âm (Pronunciation): âm cuối rõ (-s, -ed, -t, -k), trọng âm từ đúng, nhấn vào từ mang thông tin chính, ngữ điệu lên xuống tự nhiên; người nghe hiểu dễ dàng suốt bài.
Tự chấm nhanh: trả lời chỉ 1 câu ngắn hoặc ngập ngừng liên tục → khoảng band 5; trả lời có mở rộng, đôi lúc tìm từ, có vài lỗi → band 6–6.5; nói tự nhiên, có cụm từ hay, lỗi hiếm → band 7–8.

sections.intro: Bạn có 1 phút chuẩn bị (được ghi chú từ khóa) và nói liên tục 1–2 phút về chủ đề trong thẻ đề. Cố gắng nói đủ cả 4 ý và kéo dài gần 2 phút. Ghi âm, bấm giờ, rồi so sánh với bài mẫu.

tasks.p:
Describe a practical skill that you learned from an older person.
You should say:
• what the skill is
• who taught it to you
• how you learned it
and explain how you feel about having this skill.
tasks.model:
I'd like to talk about how I learned to make bánh chưng, the square sticky rice cakes that families in Vietnam traditionally prepare for the Lunar New Year. The person who taught me was my grandmother, who has been making them for over sixty years and is something of a legend in our neighbourhood.

I must have been about twelve when she decided I was old enough to help properly. Up until then, my job had simply been to wash the dong leaves, the large green leaves we wrap the cakes in. That year, though, she sat me down beside her on a low stool in the yard and showed me the whole process step by step: how to soak the rice overnight, how to season the pork with nothing more than salt and pepper, and, hardest of all, how to fold the leaves into a perfectly square shape and tie them tightly with strips of bamboo. She refused to let me use a wooden mould, as a lot of people do nowadays; she insisted that I learn to do it entirely by hand. My first few attempts were a complete disaster, lopsided and so loose that the rice leaked out while they were boiling. But she was incredibly patient, and by the end of the afternoon I'd made a couple that she declared good enough to give to the neighbours.

As for how I feel about it, I'm genuinely proud. It isn't a skill I use often, only once a year, but every time I wrap a cake, I feel connected to my grandmother and to a tradition that goes back generations. I've actually started teaching my younger cousins, so in a way, I'm passing on what she gave me.
tips: Trong 1 phút chuẩn bị, ghi 3–4 từ khóa cho mỗi gạch đầu dòng, không viết cả câu.
Dùng thì quá khứ đúng (must have been, had simply been, showed, declared) và chuyển sang hiện tại ở phần cảm nghĩ.
Phần ‘explain how you feel’ là chỗ ghi điểm – nói cảm xúc thật, có lý do.

rubric: Trôi chảy & mạch lạc: nói liên tục khoảng 1 phút 45 giây – 2 phút, có trình tự rõ (giới thiệu → diễn biến → cảm nghĩ), ít ngắt quãng dài. Nói dưới 1 phút 30 giây thường khó đạt band 7.
Vốn từ: từ ngữ cụ thể, sinh động cho chủ đề (soak, season, fold, lopsided, leak out, pass on); biết giải thích từ tiếng Việt bằng tiếng Anh (bánh chưng → square sticky rice cakes).
Ngữ pháp: kể chuyện quá khứ chính xác (quá khứ đơn, quá khứ hoàn thành, must have + V3), có câu phức và mệnh đề quan hệ; ít lỗi.
Phát âm: rõ ràng, ngữ điệu kể chuyện tự nhiên, nhấn mạnh từ cảm xúc (genuinely proud, complete disaster).

sections.intro: Giám khảo hỏi các câu mang tính khái quát, liên quan đến chủ đề Part 2 (truyền dạy kỹ năng giữa các thế hệ). Câu trả lời nên dài hơn Part 1 (khoảng 4–6 câu): nêu quan điểm → lý do → ví dụ → so sánh/nhượng bộ → kết luận ngắn.

tasks.p: What kinds of skills do older people typically pass on to younger generations in your country?
tasks.model: In Vietnam, I'd say the most common ones are domestic skills, particularly cooking traditional dishes, which tend to be learned by watching rather than from written recipes. In rural areas, older people also pass on farming knowledge, such as when to plant certain crops or how to read changes in the weather. And beyond practical skills, there's a great deal of what you might call social knowledge: how to behave at family ceremonies, how to address relatives properly and so on. That kind of thing is rarely taught formally; it's absorbed through years of simply being around older family members.

tasks.p: Do you think young people today are less interested in learning traditional skills? Why?
tasks.model: To some extent, yes, but I don't think it's because they don't value them. It's more a question of time and necessity. Young people today are under enormous pressure to study and build careers, and many of them move to big cities, far away from the grandparents who might teach them. On top of that, a lot of traditional skills are no longer essential, since you can buy a perfectly good cake in a shop. That said, I've noticed something of a revival recently, with young people taking up crafts like pottery or embroidery as hobbies, partly as a reaction against spending all day staring at screens.

tasks.p: Is it better to learn a practical skill from a person or from online videos?
tasks.model: I think both have their place. Online videos are fantastic in terms of convenience: you can pause, rewind and watch an expert from anywhere in the world, often for free. But for anything that relies on touch or timing, like cooking or carpentry, a real teacher has a huge advantage, because they can spot your mistakes immediately and correct them. A video can't tell you that you're holding the knife the wrong way. So ideally, I'd use videos to get the basic idea and then practise with someone who can give me feedback.

tasks.p: Should schools spend more time teaching practical life skills, such as cooking or basic repairs?
tasks.model: I'd argue that they should, although not at the expense of core academic subjects. A surprising number of young people leave home without knowing how to cook a simple, healthy meal or manage a budget, and those gaps can really affect their well-being. Schools are in a good position to fill them, especially for children whose parents don't have the time to teach them. Perhaps the most realistic approach would be to build these skills into existing subjects, for instance by teaching budgeting in maths lessons, rather than adding extra hours to an already crowded timetable.

tasks.p: How might the skills people need change over the next twenty years?
tasks.model: It's hard to predict precisely, but I suspect that routine tasks, whether manual or clerical, will increasingly be handled by machines and artificial intelligence. As a result, the skills that matter most will probably be the ones machines struggle with: creativity, complex problem-solving and the ability to understand and work with other people. Adaptability will also be crucial, because people are likely to change jobs several times and will need to keep learning throughout their lives. Ironically, though, I think hands-on skills like plumbing or caring for the elderly may become more valuable rather than less, since they're very difficult to automate.
